summary: Describes the core ideas of the Content-Centric Networking (CCNx) architecture and a protocol built on two messages, Interests and Content Objects. It specifies the mandatory and optional fields and their behavior independent of any wire encoding. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of asking a particular computer for something, you shout what you want by name, and anyone nearby who has it can hand it back.

questions: what is an interest in content centric networking
what is a content object in ccnx
what is the pending interest table
subtitle: A network that fetches content by hierarchical name instead of by host address, using Interests and Content Objects.

tldr.problem: Normal networks send requests to an endpoint address. CCNx wants to name content itself and fetch it from whoever on the path can supply it, with integrity that does not depend on the channel or host.
tldr.mechanism: A consumer sends an Interest carrying a hierarchical name, optionally restricted by signer KeyId or Content Object hash. Forwarders route it by longest name-prefix match, keep return state, and send back a matching Content Object.
tldr.outcome: The document defines the semantics only, independent of wire encoding. It is an Experimental protocol from the IRTF, not an IETF standard.

today: RFC 8569 is Experimental and has not been obsoleted or updated. It is published under the IRTF, not as an IETF standard, and its TLV wire encoding is defined in RFC 8609.

sections.title: Introduction and Architecture
sections.content:
CCNx uses a hierarchical name to forward requests and to match responses to requests. It does not use endpoint addresses such as IP. Every forwarder along the path does the name matching and restriction checking. The protocol fits within the Information-Centric Networking framework of RFC 7927, and the TLV wire encoding is in RFC 8609.

A producer (or publisher) wraps content in Content Objects and signs them. A consumer asks for a name by sending an Interest and gets back a Content Object or an Interest Return control message. A Forwarding Information Base (FIB) tells a forwarder where to send a request. This document describes CCNx 1.0, which differs from the earlier CCNx 0.x in that a response name must exactly equal the request name; content discovery is left to higher-layer protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: You ask for something by its name, like calling out a book title in a library. Helpers pass the request along until someone has the book and passes it back.

sections.title: Messages and Their Fields
sections.content:
There are three message types: Interest, Content Object and Interest Return. The RFC gives an ABNF grammar that is independent of any wire encoding. An Interest has a hop limit, an optional lifetime and a Name. A Content Object has an optional name, optional fields such as ExpiryTime and PayloadType, and an optional payload. Either may carry a Validation section.

The two restrictions an Interest may carry are the KeyIdRestr (limits responses to those signed by a given key) and the ContentObjectHashRestr (limits responses to one whose hash matches; it MUST use SHA256-32). A name is a nonempty first segment followed by zero or more segments, each a type plus opaque octets compared in binary. Absolute times are 64-bit UTC milliseconds.

If no Lifetime is given the default is 2 seconds, and a consumer SHOULD set the hop limit reasonably or use the default of 255.
sections.plainLanguage: A request is like a note with the name of what you want, a time limit, and a limit on how many helpers it may pass through. The answer is a package with its own signature.

sections.title: How Forwarders Behave
sections.content:
Interest processing runs through the HopLimit check, optional validation, aggregation, a Content Store lookup, then a FIB lookup by longest prefix match, segment by segment. The hop limit is decremented at each hop, and an Interest with a received hop limit of 0 from a remote system is discarded.

The notional Pending Interest Table (PIT) records the last hop plus the name and restrictions, so a Content Object can find its way back without a return address. Similar Interests (same Name, KeyIdRestr and ContentObjectHashRestr) can be aggregated, so one response satisfies several requesters. An Interest from the same previous hop MUST be forwarded again as a retransmission. A real PIT is not mandated, only the external behavior.

The Content Store is an optional cache. It MUST NOT answer a KeyId-restricted Interest unless it knows the signature is correct, and it MUST NOT answer a hash-restricted Interest unless it knows the hash is correct. In both cases failing that, it treats the Interest as a cache miss. A Content Object SHOULD only be cached if it satisfied an Interest, to reduce cache poisoning.
sections.plainLanguage: Each helper remembers who asked for what, so the answer can go back the way the question came. If two people ask the same thing, one answer is shared.

sections.title: Names, Hashes and Validation
sections.content:
A name can be a prefix name, an exact name or a full name (an exact name plus a Content Object hash). Cache control uses two fields: ExpiryTime inside the signed envelope, after which the object MUST no longer be used from a cache, and the Recommended Cache Time outside it, a hint that caching has low value.

Integrity travels with the data. Validation can be a signature (RSA-SHA256, EC-SECP-256K1 or EC-SECP-384R1), a MAC (HMAC-SHA256) or a message integrity code (CRC32C). The KeyId is a hash of the DER-encoded public key, and all implementations MUST support SHA-256 for it. A KeyLink names where to fetch the key.

A Content Object satisfies an Interest only if its name (when present) equals the Interest name, its KeyId equals the KeyId restriction (when present), and its hash equals the hash restriction (when present). A nameless object must match on at least the hash.
sections.plainLanguage: Each package is signed by its maker, so you can trust it no matter who handed it to you. Matching rules make sure you only get the package you asked for.

sections.title: Interest Return
sections.content:
An Interest Return sends an Interest back to the previous hop when a node cannot handle it. It is a 1-hop message and tells the previous hop to expect no response from that node. It is the Interest with two changes: the packet type is set to Interest Return and the return code is set. A forwarder is not required to send or process any of them.

The reasons defined are No Route, HopLimit Exceeded, Interest MTU Too Large, No Resources, Path Error, Prohibited, Congestion, Unsupported Content Object Hash Algorithm and Malformed Interest. A receiving forwarder can try a different path, never reusing the same path, or pass an Interest Return back along the reverse path. Other error paths are an application-level error from the producer and a plain consumer timeout.
sections.plainLanguage: If a helper cannot pass your note on, it hands the note back with a reason, like "no road that way", so you can try something else.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
CCNx is a layer 3 protocol with built-in authentication by signature or MAC, or an integrity check instead. It specifies no encryption envelope; that is left to a higher layer. Trust in keys is also outside its scope.

Signing or authenticating an Interest does not make it secure, and expensive validation on Interests could enable computational denial of service. An application might use a MIC on an Interest to detect corruption. Cache poisoning is the main concern for Content Stores, and CCNx 1.0 has no way to exclude bad results. The signature-restricted case needs the closest attention: the Content Store must only respond if it can verify the signature. The Interest Return has no authenticator from the previous hop, so a node should check that it really sent that Interest.

CCNx names are compared in binary, unlike URI hostnames, so variants such as differing case could enable phishing unless URI normalization and routing conventions address it. The document has no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: Signatures prove who made something, but they do not hide it. Caches must check signatures before sharing, or one bad copy could be handed to everyone.

messages.label: Interest (Name)
messages.note: Forwarder records the last hop in its PIT.

messages.label: Interest (HopLimit decremented)
messages.note: Chosen by longest prefix match in the FIB.

messages.label: Content Object
messages.note: Sent to each last hop in the matching PIT entries.

items.label: No Route
items.desc: The returning forwarder has no route to the Interest name.

items.label: HopLimit Exceeded
items.desc: The HopLimit has decremented to 0 and the packet needs to be forwarded.

items.label: Interest MTU too large
items.desc: The Interest's MTU does not conform to the required minimum and would require fragmentation.

items.label: No Resources
items.desc: The node does not have the resources to process the Interest.

items.label: Path error
items.desc: A transient transmission error while forwarding along a route.

items.label: Prohibited
items.desc: An administrative setting prohibits processing this Interest.

items.label: Congestion
items.desc: The Interest was dropped due to congestion (a transient error).

items.label: Unsupported Content Object Hash Algorithm
items.desc: The hash restriction uses an algorithm that cannot be computed.

items.label: Malformed Interest
items.desc: The Interest was dropped because it did not correctly parse.
